title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:27–31)
hook: on the road he turns to the weeping women

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's mockery: a ruler who wanted a show and got silence. Your line was silence before Herod. Now a new week, on the road to the cross.

On the wall of a parish church hangs the eighth of the traditional Stations of the Cross: Jesus meets the women of Jerusalem. Often it's a carved panel, a bent figure with the cross and a few women with their hands to their faces. The scene comes from Luke alone. The sentence has been passed. Jesus is being led away, and the soldiers have seized a man named Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, to carry the cross behind him. A great crowd follows, and among them women who bewail and lament him. He stops, turns, and speaks to them.
screen: `THE EIGHTH STATION.` → `SIMON CARRIES THE CROSS.` → `WOMEN MOURNING ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." It's startling from a man on his way to be crucified. Someone else carries his cross, and his attention goes outward, to the people beside the road and to what is coming for their city. Luke has prepared us: a few chapters back, Jesus wept over Jerusalem as he rode toward it. Now he turns the women's tears the same way. He speaks of days when people will call the childless blessed, and ask the mountains to fall on them. Then a proverb readers still turn over: "For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood doesn't catch easily; dry wood does. One common reading: if they do this to the innocent one, what will happen when the times get truly dry and hard? Some readers connect the warning with the later Roman destruction of Jerusalem. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't brush the women off or call their tears wrong. He takes them seriously enough to answer, and points their grief at the people they love. The scene became a station on the Way of the Cross, and it shows something hard to fake: in the middle of his own suffering, he still sees the people in front of him.
screen: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.` · `WEEP FOR YOUR CHILDREN.` · `GREEN WOOD AND DRY.` · `HE STILL SEES THEM.`

segments.voice: Let whatever is heavy for you right now be there; don't push it away. Then, gently, look past it to one face near you this week, a tired coworker, a quiet kid, a parent who changed the subject, and hold it next to your own trouble, not instead of it. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just keep them in mind a while.
Green wood. Jesus' proverb to the weeping women on the road to his death: if they do this in the green wood, what in the dry? Today's word.
Your line: weep for yourselves. Even on that road, he turned toward them. Rest well.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, walking from one image to the next around the church; the eighth station is Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

chat.says: Why did Jesus tell the women not to cry for him? Wasn't that a bit cold?
options: He took their tears seriously and turned them toward their own city and children.
He was telling them to go home, since women weren't allowed to follow him.
He meant they should be glad instead, because his suffering was nearly over.
chat.meaning: He answered their tears: weep for yourselves, and for your children. Even on the road to the cross, he still saw them.
